meta_description: What to do if insurance missed roof damage: document it, get a roofer's report, request a reinspection and use appraisal if needed. Free claim reviews.
h1: What to Do If Insurance Missed Roof Damage
primary_keyword: what to do if insurance missed roof damage
excerpt: Insurance missed part of your roof damage? Learn how to document it, request a reinspection or supplement, track Texas deadlines and use appraisal if needed.
key_takeaways: Missed roof damage is common after large Texas storms and can still be addressed.
Document missed damage before any permanent repairs are made.
Request a reinspection in writing with a roofer's line-item estimate and photos.
Track Chapter 542 deadlines and your policy's time limits.
Appraisal can resolve missed scope and pricing when coverage is accepted.
body_html:
Wondering what to do if insurance missed roof damage? Document the missed damage right away, get a line-item report from a qualified roofer, compare it to the carrier's estimate, and request a reinspection or supplement in writing. If the carrier still will not correct the scope, the appraisal clause in most Texas policies can resolve the dispute.

An insurance inspection is supposed to catch every damaged component, but it often does not. Many Texas homeowners learn about missed roof damage only when a roofer takes a closer look, a leak appears months later, or new damage turns up during tear-off. The good news is that a completed inspection or even a payment does not necessarily end your options. Here is what to do, step by step.

Why does insurance miss roof damage?

High claim volume after major storms

After a large hailstorm in Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin or San Antonio, carriers may receive thousands of claims in days. Adjusters, many brought in from out of state, work long hours under pressure to close files. Short inspections make missed damage more likely.

Not all roof damage is obvious

Hail bruising may not be visible until you press on the shingle. Wind-lifted shingles can settle back down after breaking their seal strips. Flashing failures and damaged underlayment hide beneath other materials. These forms of damage require hands-on inspection, not a quick look.

Inspection limitations

Steep pitch, height, wet conditions or safety rules may keep an adjuster off part of the roof. Some inspections rely on drone images or aerial measurements, which are useful for dimensions but cannot confirm bruising or broken seals. Texas makes this worse. Hail is common along the I-35 corridor, in the Panhandle and across North Texas, and storms often hit the same neighborhoods more than once in a season. When a second storm follows the first, carriers may question which event caused which damage, so missed damage that is not documented promptly becomes harder to prove. Our guide to why insurance companies underscope roof damage explains these causes in more depth.

What roof damage do insurance companies commonly miss?

Missed damageWhy it is missedHow to document it
Hail bruising and fractured matsNot visible without touchClose-up photos with chalk circles and scale, test squares on every slope
Wind-creased and unsealed shinglesShingles lie flat after the stormPhotos of creases and broken seals, lift tests by a roofer
Flashing damageHidden or assumed reusablePhotos at walls, chimneys, skylights and valleys
Vents, pipe jacks and capsTreated as minor accessoriesPhotos of dents, cracks and splits
Collateral damageNot tied back to the roof claimDented gutters, downspouts, screens and AC fins
Interior damage from roof leaksAppears days or weeks laterDated photos of stains, attic moisture readings

Flashing deserves special attention. It is one of the most frequently missed components because adjusters often assume step and counter flashing can be reused, even though it usually cannot be removed and reset without damage. Collateral damage to soft metals is also valuable because it helps confirm hail size and direction.

What are the warning signs your roof claim is incomplete?

  • Your contractor's findings exceed the insurance scope. If a roofer finds damage on slopes or components the carrier did not include, ask why.
  • Roofing components are missing from the estimate. No starter, ridge cap, drip edge, vents or flashing is a red flag.
  • New damage appears during repairs. Rotted decking or damaged underlayment found during tear-off belongs in a supplement.
  • Leaks continue after the settlement. Ongoing leaks often point to damage that was never repaired.

For a broader checklist, see signs your insurance claim was underpaid.

What should you do immediately after discovering missed roof damage?

  1. Document everything. Take date-stamped photos and video of every slope, accessory and interior stain. Include wide shots for context and close-ups with a ruler or coin for scale.
  2. Get detailed contractor documentation. Ask your roofer for a written report and, ideally, a line-item estimate that mirrors the carrier's format.
  3. Review the insurance estimate carefully. Check measurements, pitch, waste factor and every line item. Make sure the roof size and pitch match an independent measurement.
  4. Protect the property. Tarp active leaks and dry interior areas. Keep receipts for reasonable mitigation costs.
  5. Organize your records. Keep the claim number, adjuster contacts, estimates, letters and photos in one place. Our claim documentation checklist can help.
Tip: Do not let anyone complete permanent repairs before missed damage is documented and the carrier has had a chance to see it. Once the evidence is gone, the argument usually goes with it.

How do you challenge an incomplete roof damage assessment?

Contact the insurance company in writing

Notify the carrier that you have found additional damage, explain what was missed and attach your evidence. Ask for a revised estimate or a supplemental payment. Written communication creates a clear record and triggers the carrier's obligation to respond.

Request a reinspection

Ask the carrier to send an adjuster back out, and have your roofer present. Walk the adjuster to each missed item. Many disputes end here when the adjuster sees the damage in person. If the carrier sends a different adjuster or an engineer, ask for a copy of their report and photos afterward so you can respond point by point.

Submit additional evidence

Provide your roofer's line-item estimate, photos, measurement reports, manufacturer installation requirements and any local code requirements. The more specific your evidence, the harder it is to dismiss.

Track Texas deadlines

Under Texas Insurance Code Chapter 542, carriers generally must accept or reject a claim within 15 business days after receiving the information they requested, with extensions in some circumstances. Your policy may also set limits on reopening claims or filing suit. Use our Texas claim deadline calculator to keep track. This is general information, not legal advice.

What if a reinspection does not solve the problem?

If the carrier agrees the roof was damaged by a covered storm but will not include the missed items or pay a fair price for them, the dispute is about the amount of loss. That is exactly what the appraisal clause in most Texas homeowners policies is designed to resolve. Our article on whether appraisal can reopen a closed insurance claim covers situations where the claim was already paid and closed.

How does the insurance appraisal process work for missed roof damage?

Either party can usually demand appraisal in writing. Each side then appoints a competent, disinterested appraiser. The two appraisers inspect the roof, review the evidence and try to agree on the amount of loss. If they cannot agree, an umpire decides the disputed items, and an award signed by any two of the three generally sets the amount.

  • The appraiser's role: inspect, document and write a complete scope, then negotiate with the other appraiser. Your appraiser advocates for an accurate, fully supported number, backed by photos and a line-item estimate.
  • The umpire's role: resolve only the items the appraisers cannot agree on. See what does an insurance umpire do.

Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), Texas appraisers can decide the amount of loss and evaluate the extent and cause of damage, but they do not decide coverage. Missed slopes, missing line items and pricing disputes are well suited to appraisal.

How to strengthen your position before appraisal

  • Get an independent roof evaluation that covers every slope, accessory and elevation, not just the obvious damage.
  • Gather extensive photos including test squares, soft-metal dents and interior stains, each labeled by location.
  • Preserve physical evidence such as a damaged shingle, vent cap or piece of flashing removed during repairs.
  • Understand your policy language, especially the appraisal clause, loss settlement terms and any cosmetic or roof surface endorsement.
  • Keep organized records so your appraiser can see the full history of the claim at a glance.

Strong preparation shortens appraisal and gives your appraiser the evidence needed to defend each line item in front of the other appraiser or the umpire.

When does hiring an insurance appraiser make sense?

  • The roof claim is large or involves a full replacement.
  • Hail damage is extensive across many slopes or structures.
  • The gap between your roofer's estimate and the carrier's estimate is significant.
  • Multiple structures such as detached garages, barns or fences are affected.
  • The dispute has dragged on through several reinspections.

Our appraisal cost calculator helps you weigh the likely cost of appraisal against the amount in dispute.

Common mistakes after insurance misses roof damage

  • Accepting the first settlement without comparing it to an independent estimate.
  • Skipping an independent roof inspection.
  • Waiting months to act, which invites arguments about later storms or neglect.
  • Relying on phone calls instead of written requests.
  • Completing repairs before documenting missed damage.
  • Not reading the policy, including the appraisal clause and any cosmetic damage endorsement.

Next steps for Texas homeowners

Missed roof damage is common, and it is fixable when you act quickly and document well. Start with a thorough roofer inspection, put your evidence in writing to the carrier, and request a reinspection with your roofer on site to point out each missed item. If that does not work, consider appraisal.

faqs.q: Can I reopen my roof claim if the adjuster missed damage?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many carriers will accept a supplement or reopen a claim when you provide new evidence of damage from the same storm, such as a roofer's report and photos. Policy terms and time limits vary, so act promptly, put your request in writing and keep copies of everything you send.

faqs.q: How do I ask for a second roof inspection?
faqs.a: Send the carrier a written request explaining what was missed, attach photos and your roofer's estimate, and ask for a reinspection with your roofer present. Keep a record of the date you sent it. During the visit, walk the adjuster directly to each missed item so nothing is overlooked again.

faqs.q: What if new roof damage is found during replacement?
faqs.a: Stop and document it before work continues. Photograph rotted decking, damaged underlayment or other hidden damage, and have your roofer notify the carrier with a supplemental estimate. Most carriers expect supplements for damage that could not be seen before tear-off, but they need evidence to approve them.

faqs.q: Should I hire a public adjuster or an appraiser for missed roof damage?
faqs.a: A public adjuster handles the overall claim and negotiation for a fee. An appraiser is appointed under the policy's appraisal clause to resolve a dispute over the amount of loss. If the carrier accepts that the storm damaged your roof but disputes the scope or price, appraisal is often the more direct path.

faqs.q: How long does it take to resolve a missed roof damage dispute?
faqs.a: A reinspection and revised estimate may take a few weeks. If the dispute moves to appraisal, many residential roof appraisals resolve within a few months, depending on how quickly appraisers are appointed, whether an umpire is needed and how responsive both sides are.
